new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent falls on the antepenultimate syllable ('the last syllable but two'); Hocart hedges that a long penult may instead attract the accent (a possible weight-based override). He also reports that k, m, n, t are lengthened (geminated) after the accented syllable, giving forms like rikko, tammu, maranni, ngetto. Note that the gemination examples are two- and three-syllable words where the lengthened consonant follows the penult, so the examples sit uneasily with the antepenult statement; the source does not resolve this.
new_statements.exceptions: 'except, perhaps, when the last but one is long' (long penult may carry the accent). Spelling of vowels and of g/v/w is stated to be uncertain.
new_statements.domain_note: General statement about 'the language' of Eddystone Island (Mandegusu = Simbo) from the 1908 Percy Sladen Trust fieldwork of Hocart and Rivers; word level implied (examples are isolated words and names); no citation-form vs phrase distinction is made. The author is an anthropologist writing an ethnographic paper, not a phonological description; the statement is hedged and over a century old.
new_statements.identity_note: Hocart 1922 describes the language of 'Eddystone Island', native name Mandegusu ('the four villages'), of which Simbo is one district; Ray 1926 and Palmer 1996 confirm Eddystone = Mandegusu = Simbo, i.e. simb1256 (ISO sbb). No dialect is specified; data are from the 1908 Hocart-Rivers fieldwork on the island. Glottolog's third ref (Pat 1996, Hula) is a mis-association with a PNG language and was ignored.
